text:
I had gone too far to turn back, and besides, this girl overwhelmed me. This mixture of gaiety, sadness, innocence, prostitution, even this illness, which was bound to heighten in her the sensitivity of her impressions as well as the irritability of her nerves—everything made me understand that if, from the very first, I did not gain some hold over this forgetful and flighty nature, she was lost to me.

“Come now, is what you are saying really serious?” she said.

“Very serious.”

“But why did you not tell me this sooner?”

“When could I have told you?”

“The day after you were introduced to me at the Opéra-Comique.”

“I think you would have received me very badly if I had come to see you.”

“Why?”

“Because I had been stupid the night before.”

“That is true. But even so, you already loved me then?”

“Yes.”

“Which did not prevent you from going to bed and sleeping quite peacefully after the performance. We know what these great loves are like.”

“Well, that is where you are mistaken. Do you know what I did on the evening of the Opéra-Comique?”

“No.”

“I waited for you at the door of the Café Anglais. I followed the carriage that took you and your three friends away, and when I saw you alight alone and go into your home alone, I was very happy.”

Marguerite began to laugh.

“What are you laughing at?”

“Nothing.”

“Tell me, I beg you, or I shall think that you are making fun of me again.”

“You will not be angry?”

“What right would I have to be angry?”

“Well, there was a good reason why I went home alone.”

“What was it?”

“Someone was waiting for me here.”

Had she stabbed me with a knife, she could not have hurt me more. I rose and, holding out my hand to her, said:

“Goodbye.”

“I knew you would be angry,” she said. “Men have a mania for wanting to learn what is bound to cause them pain.”

“But I assure you,” I added in a cold tone, as though I had wished to prove that I was forever cured of my passion, “I assure you that I am not angry. It was perfectly natural for someone to be waiting for you, just as it is perfectly natural for me to leave at three in the morning.”

“Do you too have someone waiting for you at home?”

“No, but I must go.”

“Goodbye, then.”

“Are you sending me away?”

“Not in the least.”

“Why are you hurting me?”

“How have I hurt you?”

“You tell me that someone was waiting for you.”

“I could not help laughing at the thought that you had been so happy to see me go home alone, when there was such a good reason for it.”

“We often make a joy of some childish trifle, and it is cruel to destroy that joy when, by allowing it to remain, one can make the person who finds it happier still.”

“But who do you think you are dealing with? I am neither a virgin nor a duchess. I have known you only since today, and I owe you no account of my actions. Even supposing that one day I become your mistress, you must understand that I have had other lovers besides you. If you are already making jealous scenes before then, what will it be afterward, if there ever is an afterward? I have never seen a man like you.”

“That is because no one has ever loved you as I love you.”

“Come now, honestly, do you really love me so much?”

“As much as it is possible to love, I believe.”

“And this has lasted since...?”

“Since a day when I saw you alight from a carriage and enter Susse’s, three years ago.”

“Do you know that that is very beautiful? Well, what must I do to acknowledge this great love?”

“You must love me a little,” I said, with a pounding heart that almost prevented me from speaking; for, despite the half-mocking smiles with which she had accompanied this entire conversation, it seemed to me that Marguerite was beginning to share my agitation and that I was approaching the hour I had awaited for so long.

“Well, and the duke?”

“What duke?”

“My jealous old man.”

“He will know nothing about it.”

“And if he does find out?”

“He will forgive you.”

“Oh, no! He will abandon me, and what will become of me?”

“You do risk his abandoning you for someone else.”

“How do you know?”

“From the instruction you gave that no one was to be admitted tonight.”

“That is true; but that man is a serious friend.”

“One for whom you care very little, since you have your door barred to him at such an hour.”

“You are hardly the one to reproach me for that, since it was in order to receive you and your friend.”

Little by little I had drawn closer to Marguerite; I had put my hands around her waist, and I could feel her supple body resting lightly upon my clasped hands.

“If you only knew how I love you!” I said to her in a low voice.

“Truly?”

“I swear it to you.”

“Well, if you promise to do everything I wish without saying a word, without raising an objection, without questioning me, perhaps I shall love you.”

“Anything you wish!”

“But I warn you, I want to be free to do whatever I please, without giving you the slightest detail about my life. For a long time I have been looking for a young lover, without a will of his own, loving without mistrust, loved without rights. I have never been able to find one. Men, instead of being satisfied that they are granted for a long time what they would scarcely have hoped to obtain once, demand from their mistress an account of the present, the past, and even the future. As they grow accustomed to her, they want to dominate her, and they become all the more demanding the more they are given everything they want. If I decide to take a new lover now, I want him to possess three very rare qualities: I want him to be trusting, submissive, and discreet.”

“Well, I shall be everything you wish.”

“We shall see.”

“And when shall we see?”

“Later.”

“Why?”

“Because,” said Marguerite, freeing herself from my arms and taking from a large bouquet of red camellias brought that morning a camellia which she put in my buttonhole, “because treaties cannot always be carried out on the day they are signed. That is easy to understand.”

“And when shall I see you again?” I said, clasping her in my arms.

“When this camellia changes color.”

“And when will it change color?”

“Tomorrow, between eleven and midnight. Are you satisfied?”
